title: How Chile Can Turn U.S.-China Rivalry into Negotiating Power
gist: Chile's new Kast government has publicly named the US its main strategic partner while China absorbs 53% of its copper exports and 70% of its lithium — a dependency the author argues is two-way leverage rather than pure vulnerability, given Chile holds the world's largest lithium reserves and is the second-largest copper producer. The recommended play is an explicit, bounded investment-screening regime plus diversification into India, the Gulf and ASEAN, after Washington's pressure over a Chinese-linked Hong Kong-Valparaíso submarine cable and visa bans on three outgoing Boric officials showed the US will squeeze even friendly partners.

themes.theme: Chile's China dependency in hard numbers

insights.claim: China absorbs 53% of Chile's copper exports and 70% of its lithium, the two pillars of the country's economic future, and no other Latin American country sends a higher share of its exports to China.
insights.speaker: Andrés Villar
insights.so_what: Quantifies the single largest transmission channel from Chinese industrial demand to Chilean fiscal and FX outcomes; a China slowdown hits Chile harder than any other LatAm economy.
insights.locator: But as the new government makes this a priority

insights.claim: Chile holds the world's largest lithium reserves and is the second-largest copper producer, at a time when the US and Western allies urgently need both metals to sustain their energy transitions.
insights.speaker: Andrés Villar
insights.so_what: Chile is a structural bottleneck for Western electrification; any Chilean policy change on ownership, royalties or processing has global cost-curve implications.
insights.locator: The U.S. and Western allies, for their part, urgently need copper

insights.claim: Chile's foreign minister Francisco Pérez Mackenna publicly called the United States 'probably, from a strategic standpoint, our main partner' while immediately adding that China remains a tremendous partner and that Chile should seek alternatives such as India.
insights.speaker: Andrés Villar
insights.so_what: First explicit ranking of the US above China by a Chilean government — a tone shift worth tracking for Chinese retaliation or investment-approval friction.
insights.quote: The United States is probably, from a strategic standpoint, our main partner

insights.claim: Chile's conservative Kast administration held its first foreign-minister-level meeting with Secretary of State Marco Rubio on July 6, with regional security and critical minerals on the agenda, as it seeks to signal alignment with the West.
insights.speaker: Andrés Villar
insights.so_what: Critical minerals are now an explicit bilateral negotiating item; watch for US offtake, financing or processing incentives directed at Chilean copper and lithium.
insights.locator: Days before the interview, on July 6

insights.claim: Chile faced pointed US pressure over a proposed transpacific submarine fiber optic cable in which Chinese companies had sought a key role, following earlier disputes over a satellite ground station and a passport procurement tender.
insights.speaker: Andrés Villar
insights.so_what: Digital and dual-use infrastructure tenders in LatAm now carry veto risk from Washington; bidders and financiers should price political disqualification.
insights.locator: The meeting between Pérez Mackenna and Rubio took place

insights.claim: In February the US alleged that the proposed Hong Kong-Valparaíso submarine cable undermined regional security and announced visa restrictions on three members of the outgoing Gabriel Boric administration, showing Washington will apply leverage even against partners it considers friendly.
insights.speaker: Andrés Villar
insights.so_what: Personal sanctions against officials of a friendly democracy is an escalation template — raises the political cost of any China-linked infrastructure decision across the region.
insights.locator: In February, the U.S. alleged that the proposed Hong Kong-Valparaíso submarine cable

insights.claim: Washington's approach under Trump has depended more on pressure than persuasion — tariffs, sanctions and explicit demands for alignment — and Chile has not been immune.
insights.speaker: Andrés Villar
insights.so_what: Assume coercion, not inducement, as the default US instrument in LatAm; alignment does not buy exemption.
insights.locator: Washington's approach under President Donald Trump

insights.claim: Chile's position is usually framed as vulnerability, but dependence works both ways: China needs Chilean copper and lithium at a time when global supply is tightening, and much of the material China processes is resold to third markets including Japan.
insights.speaker: Andrés Villar
insights.so_what: The consensus 'Chile is hostage to China' framing overstates downside; expect Chile to extract better terms rather than capitulate to either bloc.

insights.claim: Australia serves as the precedent for commodity leverage: during the 2020 trade war China never stopped buying Australian iron ore, implying Beijing will not weaponize purchases of inputs it genuinely needs.
insights.speaker: Andrés Villar
insights.so_what: A testable rule for pricing Chinese trade coercion risk: essential, hard-to-substitute inputs are effectively exempt from Chinese retaliation lists.
insights.quote: During a trade war in 2020, China never stopped buying Australian iron ore.
insights.locator: Australia serves as a useful precedent

insights.claim: The real question for Chile is not whether it has negotiating power but whether Santiago has the institutional capacity and strategic clarity to convert that power into better investment conditions, technology transfer and value-added processing rather than simply exporting raw materials to whoever applies the most pressure.
insights.speaker: Andrés Villar
insights.so_what: Watch for Chilean policy on domestic lithium/copper processing requirements — that is where resource leverage would show up as margin capture.
insights.locator: The new geopolitics of critical minerals

insights.claim: China has moved into a more selective and strategic phase in which the era of large-scale lending and infrastructure projects is giving way to targeted investment in sectors such as lithium processing and high-tech goods.
insights.speaker: Andrés Villar
insights.so_what: Expect fewer headline Chinese megaloans in LatAm and more midstream processing JVs — the value-capture fight moves downstream from mining.
insights.locator: China, meanwhile, has moved into a more selective

insights.claim: The US-China rivalry has entered a more transactional, sectoral phase — a contest for control over supply chains, critical technologies and infrastructure — which turns countries holding strategic assets into 'geopolitical swing states' with disproportionate global influence.
insights.speaker: Andrés Villar
insights.so_what: A screening frame for sovereign opportunity: identify holders of chokepoint minerals, ports and digital infrastructure, then trade their improving terms of trade.

insights.claim: Decisions that appear purely economic — a submarine cable, a satellite ground station, a passport procurement tender — can acquire geopolitical implications very quickly in Latin America.
insights.speaker: Andrés Villar
insights.so_what: Procurement risk assessment for LatAm contracts must now include great-power veto exposure, even for mundane government tenders.
insights.locator: The episode, like earlier disputes over a satellite ground station

insights.claim: There is increasing consensus among Chilean policymakers that the country needs a clear, bounded and transparent investment screening mechanism for genuinely strategic sectors, following peers in Europe and Asia, without becoming a tool of political discretion.
insights.speaker: Andrés Villar
insights.so_what: A Chilean FDI screening regime is a live legislative catalyst; it would affect deal timelines for Chinese and other foreign capital in mining, energy and digital infrastructure.

insights.claim: A state that adjusts investment criteria under external pressure introduces uncertainty and undermines long-term credibility, making ad hoc case-by-case blocking more damaging to Chile than a codified screening rule.
insights.speaker: Andrés Villar
insights.so_what: Rule-based screening is the cheaper equilibrium for Chile's cost of capital; ad hoc reversals show up as a country risk premium.
insights.quote: A state that adjusts criteria under external pressure introduces uncertainty and undermines long-term credibility.
insights.locator: The risk of inaction is real

insights.claim: Chile's reputation for openness, institutional stability and predictability remains valuable but is no longer sufficient as a standalone strategy in a fragmented international landscape.
insights.speaker: Andrés Villar
insights.so_what: Chile's traditional soft-power discount to peers may narrow if it fails to pair openness with a strategic-asset framework.
insights.locator: Chile built its international reputation on openness

insights.claim: The recommended Chilean strategy is diversification through new partnerships in the Gulf, deeper trade ties with India where a negotiation is already underway, and stronger links with ASEAN economies — not replacing China or the US.
insights.speaker: Andrés Villar
insights.so_what: A Chile-India trade negotiation in progress is a concrete, under-covered channel for redirecting copper and lithium flows.

insights.claim: The principal risk to Chile is overplaying ideological alignment with Washington and narrowing its room for maneuver with Beijing in ways that serve neither its economy nor its strategic interests.
insights.speaker: Andrés Villar
insights.so_what: Watch the Kast government for over-alignment: a sharp pro-US pivot would be the trigger for Chinese commercial retaliation against Chilean exporters.
insights.locator: Opportunity lies, then, precisely in what Pérez Mackenna signaled

insights.claim: Chile cannot fully choose sides and should not try; the challenge is not picking a dependency but building the institutional capacity and strategic clarity to manage it.
insights.speaker: Andrés Villar
insights.so_what: Base case for Chile is durable hedging, so expect policy continuity in China trade despite pro-Western rhetoric.
insights.quote: Chile cannot fully choose sides and should not try.
insights.locator: Chile's longstanding soft power remains in place
